transcript.text: Hey everyone, welcome back to Bright Circuits.
Today we're answering a question I get
all the time: how does a flat
piece of glass on a roof turn
sunlight into electricity you can actually use?
By the end of this video you'll
understand the physics inside a solar cell,
why panels are wired the way they
are, and what the inverter and battery
are really doing.
Let's start with sunlight itself. Light arrives
in tiny packets of energy called photons,
and each photon carries an amount of
energy that depends on its color. Blue
photons carry more energy than red photons,
and infrared photons carry less still. On
a clear day at noon, roughly one
thousand watts of sunlight land on every
square meter of ground. That number, one
kilowatt per square meter, is the standard
test condition every solar panel is rated
against. The whole job of a solar
panel is to catch as many of
those photons as possible and turn their
energy into moving electrons.
So what happens inside a silicon solar
cell? A solar cell is a thin
wafer of silicon that has been doped
with small amounts of other elements. The
top layer is doped with phosphorus, which
gives it extra electrons, and the bottom
layer is doped with boron, which leaves
gaps called holes. Where those two layers
meet, you get a p-n junction with
a built-in electric field. When a photon
with enough energy hits the silicon, it
knocks an electron loose and leaves a
hole behind. The electric field at the
junction pushes the electron one way and
the hole the other way, and that
separation is what creates a voltage. Connect
a wire from the front contacts to
the back contacts and the electrons flow
through it as direct current. A single
silicon cell only produces about half a
volt, no matter how big it is.
Photons with too little energy pass straight
through, and the extra energy of blue
photons is lost as heat, which is
why the best commercial cells convert only
about twenty two percent of sunlight into
electricity.
Half a volt is not very useful
on its own, so cells are combined
into panels. A typical residential panel has
sixty or seventy two cells wired in
series, which adds their voltages together to
roughly thirty to forty volts. The cells
are sandwiched between tempered glass on the
front and a polymer backsheet, then framed
in aluminum to survive decades of weather.
Because the cells are in series, shading
a single cell can drag down the
whole string, a bit like a kink
in a garden hose. That's why modern
panels include bypass diodes that let current
route around a shaded group of cells.
Panels are then wired together into strings
on the roof to reach the voltage
the inverter expects.
Now for the part most people skip:
the inverter. Solar panels produce direct current,
but your home and the electrical grid
run on alternating current. The inverter converts
direct current into alternating current that matches
the grid's voltage and frequency exactly. Good
inverters also run maximum power point tracking,
constantly adjusting the electrical load so the
panels operate at their most efficient voltage
as clouds pass and temperature changes. There
are three main options: a single string
inverter, microinverters on every panel, or power
optimizers paired with a central inverter. Microinverters
cost more, but they handle partial shading
much better because every panel is tracked
on its own. When your panels produce
more power than the house uses, the
inverter pushes the surplus onto the grid,
and with net metering your utility credits
you for it. For safety, a grid-tied
inverter shuts down automatically during a power
outage so it can't send current into
lines that utility crews are repairing.
That shutdown is exactly why batteries have
become so popular. A home battery stores
surplus solar energy during the day so
you can use it in the evening,
when demand and electricity prices are highest.
Most home batteries today use lithium iron
phosphate chemistry, which is safer and lasts
longer than the lithium chemistry in older
electric cars. A typical home battery stores
between ten and fifteen kilowatt hours, enough
to run the essentials through a night.
With a battery and the right inverter,
your system can keep the lights on
during a blackout by forming its own
small island grid. Batteries add significant cost,
though, so whether one makes sense depends
on your utility's rates and how often
the power goes out.
So, is solar worth it? For most
homes with a sunny, unshaded roof, a
solar system pays for itself in roughly
six to ten years, and panels are
usually warrantied for twenty five years. Panels
slowly lose about half a percent of
their output each year, so after twenty
five years they still produce close to
ninety percent of their original power. The
key takeaway: a solar panel is just
billions of photons knocking electrons loose in
silicon, and everything else is about collecting,
converting and storing that energy efficiently. If
this helped, check out our follow-up video
on sizing a system for your own
home, and I'll see you in the
next one.
